name: Threading kit

card.summary: Twisted-thread plucking for brows and face: precise and cheap, temporary, barely studied.
card.note: Technique has little formal research; complications are rarely discussed.

quick.overview:
Threading uses a twisted thread to pull rows of fine hairs out at the follicle, mostly to shape eyebrows and clean up facial hair. A kit lets people try the technique at home.

It is an old technique with a long salon tradition. Hair grows back, so results are temporary, and published research is limited to a review of its complications.
quick.mechanism: A doubled, twisted thread is rolled across the skin, trapping hairs and lifting them out at the root in quick succession.
quick.risks: Pain, skin irritation and other complications have been described in a dermatology review. No formal trials compare it with waxing or tweezing.

lead: Threading is a hair-removal method, used mainly on eyebrows and facial hair, in which a doubled and twisted cotton or polyester thread is rolled over unwanted hair so that it is pulled out at the follicle.[1][2] A threading kit is the consumer version of the tool: thread (sometimes with a handle or tensioning aid) that lets the technique be tried at home rather than in a salon.

People use threading to shape the eyebrows and clean up the upper lip, chin and jawline. Cleveland Clinic describes it as giving precise, sharp brow lines, and notes that because hairs come out from the root, many people return every three to four weeks.[3] Brow shape strongly frames the eyes and face, which is why threading features in brow and grooming routines.

The technique is described as an ancient practice from the Middle East and South Asia that spread to Western countries.[1][2] It is performed by hand, by mouth or around the neck, and the mouth method is described as the fastest and most precise.[2] A 2009 review in Clinical and Experimental Dermatology discussed the procedure's popularity and its seldom-discussed complications.[1] No controlled trials comparing threading with waxing or tweezing were found.

angle.text: Threading shapes brows and removes fine facial hair with a clean, defined edge. Results are temporary, so users repeat the process every few weeks.

paras: A thin thread is doubled, twisted and rolled along the skin so that rows of short hairs are caught and lifted out at once, unlike tweezing which removes hairs one at a time.[2] It is used chiefly for eyebrows, but also the upper lip, chin and jawline; sources describe it as unsuited to arms and legs, where hair is coarser and more extensive.[2][3]

Threading is described as centuries old and as having begun in the Middle East and South Asia, where it was in some places linked to rites of passage such as preparation for marriage.[2] Cleveland Clinic says it likely began in India or Iran.[3] In Taiwan, women have traditionally had facial threading before the Lunar New Year.[2] Threading salons are reported to have spread in Germany in the 1980s and to have opened in large US cities from the late 1980s, run by immigrants from the Middle East and South Asia.[2]

Cleveland Clinic lists threading as often less painful than waxing or plucking because hairs are removed quickly, gentler on skin than waxing, which can cause burns or irritation, and capable of precise lines, and it quotes dermatologist Chey Ranasinghe, MD, as saying that threading needs an experienced specialist.[3] Wikipedia credits it with finer control of eyebrow shape.[2] As an epilation method it is temporary, with hair growing back over time; Cleveland Clinic notes repeated sessions can make brow hairs thinner and slower to regrow.[3]

Threading can be painful because several hairs are pulled at once.[2] Cleveland Clinic lists redness, irritation, swelling for several hours, breakouts and a small infection risk, and notes that poor technique can cut the skin, remove the wrong hairs or pull out eyelashes. It says people using retinoids or retinol are advised to stop them five to seven days beforehand because the products make skin fragile, and that most practitioners have stopped holding the thread in the mouth, a practice that carried bacterial risk.[3] A dermatology review noted that, despite its popularity, the procedure has complications that are seldom discussed.[1]
No studies found for home threading kits. The peer-reviewed item identified is a narrative review of the salon procedure and its complications.[1]

refs.title: Eyebrow threading: a popular hair-removal procedure and its seldom-discussed complications
